newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council members grapple with Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council members grapple with Albania crisis.

text.p: Security Council members met privately on Thursday to consider a request from Italy on authorising a force to Albania, which is sliding into anarchy.
One council member said that many delegations were prepared to endorse the force in principle but needed full details before any action was taken.

"There has to be greater clarity all around," he said, including a letter from Albania on what it wanted, the duration of the mandate, details on other countries participating in the force and who would pay for it.
Greece, France, Spain, Portugal, Austria, Turkey and Romania have expressed willingness to take part.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on Thursday in Vienna said it appreciated offers from some of its members to respond to Albania's request for protection in distributing food and other necessities.

But the OSCE statement, reflecting divisions among its members, was deliberately vague. It did not endorse or set up such a force and tossed the issue to the United Nations, which also will not organise the force.
Instead, the next step will be up to Italy, which requested the council consider the issue and is expected to lead the multinational force.
But the troops would not carry emblems from the OSCE or the United Nations, diplomats said. This would be similar to the U.S.-led operation in Iraq or France's 1994 Operation Turquoise in Rwanda.
Seven members of the 15-seat Security Council also belong to the OSCE -- Britain, France, the United States, Russia, Poland and Portugal.

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding that he quit.

Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting and killing and creating a food crisis. On Thursday, 17 people died in a gun battle in Levan in central Albania in the country's most violent incident in the last two months.
Italy's U.N. ambassador, Paolo Fulci, in a letter to the council, said the issue should be considered urgently "even during the Easter holiday."
The council may consult privately over the weekend but no date for a formal meeting has been set as all members have to consult with their governments again.
Italy, not a council member this year, also drew up a draft resolution that would authorise a multi-national force.
